### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** was introduced by **Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P.** [1] to regulate the operation of computer training institutions across India [1]. According to the Statement of Objects and Reasons, the Bill addressed the proliferation of unregistered computer centres charging exorbitant fees, offering inadequate facilities or substandard course content, and abruptly shuttering operations after collecting substantial sums from enrolled students [2]. It sought to enforce mandatory registration, standardised curricula, fee controls, and penal deterrence to safeguard the student community [2].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Author / Nature:** Private Member's Bill introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P. (dated **August 18, 2004**) [1], [3].
* **Appropriate Ministry:** **Not in record.**
* **Statutory vs Executive:** Proposed statutory scheme [1].
* **Chamber / Stage:** Legislative tracking row **Not in record**; Bill text introduced as an enactment in the Fifty-fifth Year of the Republic of India [1].
* **Jurisdiction & Commencement:** Extends to the whole of India; enters into force on a date appointed by the Central Government via Official Gazette notification [1].

### 3. DESIGN

| Clause | Provision & Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Clause 1–2** | Defines "appropriate Government" as the Central Government or State Government, as the case may be [1], [4]. Defines "computer centre" as any centre conducting computer courses (including advanced education) or imparting training to those with existing skills or aspiring for jobs in IT/related sectors [4]. |
| **Clause 3** | Prohibits running any computer centre without prior registration with the appropriate Government [4]. |
| **Clause 4** | Mandates the in-charge or head of any computer centre (existing or newly established) to apply for registration within **one month** of commencement [5]. |
| **Clause 5–6** | Requires the appropriate Government to scrutinise and investigate applications to ensure the centre fulfills prescribed conditions; upon satisfaction, it issues a registration certificate for a specified period [5], [6]. |
| **Clause 7** | Empowers the appropriate Government to prescribe syllabus and fees for each course imparted [6]. |
| **Clause 8–9** | Mandates investigation of complaints regarding centre functioning, requiring a final decision within **one month** [6]. If substantiated, the appropriate Government must forthwith cancel the registration [6], [7]. |
| **Clause 11** | Empowers the Central Government to make rules by notification in the Official Gazette [2], [3]. |

### 4. PENALTIES & ADMINISTRATION
* **Administration:** Administered jointly by the **appropriate Government** (Central Government or State Government, as the case may be) [1], [4], which handles registrations, course syllabus/fee determinations, investigations, and cancellations [5], [6]. Central rulemaking power rests with the Central Government [2], [3].
* **Penalties (Clause 10):** Any person contravening the provisions of the Act faces **imprisonment for a term of not less than three years** and a **fine of not less than ₹1,00,000 (one lakh rupees)** [7].

### 5. TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For:** Eliminates fly-by-night fraudulent training centres, controls student fee exploitation, guarantees minimum infrastructure standards, and mandates a fast-track 30-day resolution window for student grievances [2], [6].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Imposes direct state-mandated syllabus and fee-setting controls on rapid-evolution technology skills [6], paired with severe mandatory minimum criminal penalties (minimum 3 years' imprisonment and ₹1 lakh fine) for operational/regulatory non-compliance [7].

### 6. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Enforcement Discretion:** Shared jurisdiction across State and Central authorities without clear demarcation of institutional tiers or inspection authorities [4], [5].
* **Price & Curriculum Freezes:** Impact of Clause 7 state-fixed curricula on fast-evolving commercial software training courses [6].
* **Enactment Status:** Bill text represents an as-introduced private member's draft; parliamentary passage status **Not in record.**

* **Case For**: Protects students from predatory commercial operators, prevents financial fraud from abrupt closures, and enforces baseline curriculum standards and fee caps [6].

* **Dual Jurisdiction**: Operational delegation between Central and State Governments for application scrutiny and enforcement under Clause 2(a) and Clause 5 [4, 11].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Essential Commodities (Second Amendment) Bill, 1986** is an amending legislative instrument aimed at democratising the enforcement of the **Essential Commodities Act, 1955** [1]. Prior to this amendment, courts could not take cognizance of offences punishable under the Act except upon a written report by a public servant [2]. The Bill expands the locus standi for instituting prosecutions by enabling an **aggrieved person** or any **recognised consumer association** to file complaints directly in court [1, 3].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
| Parameter | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Signatory / Minister** | **H. K. L. Bhagat** (Statement of Objects and Reasons dated **1st December, 1986**) [2] |
| **Ministry / Department** | **Not in record.** (The broader 1986 consumer package was associated with the Minister/Department of Food and Civil Supplies) |
| **Instrument Nature** | Statutory Central Amending Bill [1] |
| **Legislative Stage** | Enacted as Act No. **73 of 1986** (later targeted by the Repealing and Amending Bill, 1999) [4] |
| **Commencement** | Comes into force on such date as the Central Government may appoint by notification in the Official Gazette [1] |

### 3. DESIGN
* **Objectives**: Promote the voluntary consumer movement and secure active involvement of citizens and consumer bodies in enforcing commodity controls and curbing unfair distribution or pricing practices [3].
* **Amendment of Section 11**: Modifies the cognizance clause of the 1955 Act by inserting after "Indian Penal Code" the words *"or any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association, whether such person is a member of that association or not"* [1]. It adds an Explanation defining a "recognised consumer association" as a voluntary consumer association registered under the **Companies Act, 1956** or under any other law for the time being in force [2, 3].
* **Amendment of Section 12AA(1)(e)**: Inserts identical standing (*"or any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association"*) after "Government concerned" to permit complaints before Special Courts established under the special provisions framework [5, 3].
* **Penalties**: The Bill itself introduces no new penal clauses or modified sentencing scales; substantive penalties remain those already laid down under the principal Essential Commodities Act, 1955 and temporary special provisions enactments [1, 5].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For**: Removes bureaucratic gatekeeping and the sole reliance on public servants/inspectors to initiate proceedings, empowering civic organisations to hold hoarders and black-marketeers accountable [2, 3].
* **Strongest Case Against**: **Not in record.** (Parliamentary debate friction and industry objections regarding potential harassment or frivolous litigation are not recorded in the bill text).

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Gazette Commencement**: Notification of enforcement date by the Central Government [1].
* **Registration Checks**: Verification of consumer bodies against registration criteria under the Companies Act, 1956 or applicable Societies/Trusts legislation [2, 3].
* **Special Court Procedures**: Coordination with Special Courts constituted under Section 12AA for entertaining private and institutional complaints alongside official police reports [5, 3].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Essential Commodities (Second Amendment) Bill, 1986** is an amending legislative measure designed to empower consumers and consumer organisations to participate directly in the enforcement of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 [1][8]. Prior to this amendment, the principal Act did not grant individual aggrieved consumers or consumer associations the locus standi to file complaints directly in courts to initiate prosecution against contraventions [8][52]. The Bill explicitly permits courts and Special Courts to take cognizance of offences upon written complaints filed by an aggrieved person or a recognised consumer association [1][69].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsoring Authority / Signatory:** Introduced by **H. K. L. Bhagat** (Statement of Objects and Reasons dated **1st December, 1986**) [23]. Specific Ministry name: **Not in record.**
* **Legal Character:** Statutory legislation amending the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 [1].
* **Legislative Stage / Enactment Details:** Introduced in the **Lok Sabha** during the Thirty-seventh Year of the Republic of India [1][38]. Parliamentary passage date and presidential assent status: **Not in record.**
* **Commencement:** Sub-clause 1(2) specifies that it shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may appoint by notification in the Official Gazette [1].

### 3. DESIGN

| Provision | Target Section | Content and Operational Scope |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Clause 1** | Short title & Commencement | Named the **Essential Commodities (Second Amendment) Act, 1986**; comes into effect upon Central Government Gazette notification [1]. |
| **Clause 2(a)** | Section 11 of the principal Act | Inserts *"or any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association, whether such person is a member of that association or not"* after *"Indian Penal Code"*, allowing courts to take cognizance on their complaints [1]. |
| **Clause 2(b)** | Section 11 of the principal Act | Appends an Explanation defining **"recognised consumer association"** as a voluntary consumer association registered under the Companies Act, 1956 or under any other law for the time being in force [1][69]. |
| **Clause 3** | Section 12AA(1)(e) of the principal Act | Inserts *"or any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association"* after *"Government concerned"*, allowing a Special Court to take cognizance of an offence upon complaints from aggrieved persons or recognized associations without committal [8][38][69]. |

* **Funding Pattern:** Dedicated financial outlays or allocations under the Bill: **Not in record.**

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For:** Democratises enforcement of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 by removing the monopoly of public servants over initiating criminal complaints, bolstering voluntary consumer movements and consumer vigilance against black-marketing, hoarding, and illicit distribution [8][52].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Potential exposure of retail and supply chain distributors to frivolous or vexatious litigation initiated by non-state actors or rival trade interests: **Not in record** *(inference: expanding locus standi beyond designated public servants increases procedural scrutiny on commercial distributors)*.
* **Penalties in the Bill:** Specific monetary or custodial penal provisions created by the 1986 Amendment Bill itself: **Not in record.** (The Bill amends procedural cognizance provisions under Sections 11 and 12AA rather than the substantive penal sections of the 1955 Act) [1][69].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Cognizance Procedures:** Operational integration between regular Magistrates' courts under Section 11 and Special Courts established under Section 12AA upon receipt of private consumer complaints [1][38][69].
* **Registration Verification:** Procedural checks to confirm that complaining consumer bodies qualify as voluntary associations registered under the Companies Act, 1956 or corresponding prevailing laws [69].
* **Who Administers It:** Specifically designated administrative agency or department assigned in the text: **Not in record.** Central Government possesses notification powers for commencement [1], while enforcement is decentralized across the judiciary, Special Courts, public servants, aggrieved consumers, and registered consumer bodies [1][69].

### WHAT IT IS

**The Essential Commodities (Second Amendment) Bill, 1986** was introduced in the Lok Sabha to amend the **Essential Commodities Act, 1955** [1, 2]. Its core purpose was to empower consumers and support the voluntary consumer movement by giving an aggrieved person or any recognised consumer association the legal right to file complaints directly in courts regarding offences under the Act, breaking the prior statutory bar where only designated public servants or authorised officials could trigger judicial cognizance [1, 3, 4].

---

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS

| Item | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Sponsor / Signatory** | **H. K. L. Bhagat**, Minister [2] |
| **Administrative Ministry** | Ministry in charge of Essential Commodities / Civil Supplies (**Ministry name not in record**; H. K. L. Bhagat signed on **1st December, 1986**) [2] |
| **Instrument Type** | Amending Bill (Statutory) [1] |
| **Chamber & Stage** | Lok Sabha, As Introduced (**Date of introduction: 1st December, 1986**; final passage status in this desk: **Not in record**) [1, 2] |
| **Commencement Clause** | Clause 1(2): Comes into force on such date as the Central Government may appoint by notification in the Official Gazette [1] |

---

### DESIGN

The Bill contains **3 clauses** amending procedural sections of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955:

* **Clause 1**: Short title and commencement provision [1].
* **Clause 2 (Amending Section 11)**:
  * Inserts words enabling courts to take cognizance of an offence not only on the report of a public servant under section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, but also upon a report/complaint made by *"any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association, whether such person is a member of that association or not"* [1].
  * Adds an *Explanation* defining **"recognised consumer association"** as *"a voluntary consumer association registered under the Companies Act, 1956 or under any other law for the time being in force"* [4].
* **Clause 3 (Amending Section 12AA(1)(e))**:
  * Inserts the words *"or any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association"* after *"Government concerned"*, thereby empowering Special Courts to take cognizance of an offence upon a complaint made by an aggrieved person or a recognised consumer association without committal for trial [2, 4].

---

### PENALTIES & ENFORCEMENT

* **Penalties in the Bill**: **Not in record.** The Bill does not create new penal sanctions, change existing prison terms, or amend fine schedules. It solely amends cognizance rules under Section 11 and Section 12AA to broaden the category of complainants [1, 4]. Substantive penalties remain governed by the principal Essential Commodities Act, 1955 [1, 3].
* **Who Administers It**: Enforcement and cognizance powers are exercised through **Courts / Special Courts** established under the Act upon complaints filed by public servants, authorized government officers, aggrieved individuals, or registered consumer associations [1, 2, 4].

---

### TRADE-OFFS

* **Strongest Case For**: Broadens access to justice and enforcement mechanisms against black marketing, hoarding, and supply malpractice by ending the monopoly of state inspectors over prosecution and allowing organised consumer groups to directly approach courts [3, 4].
* **Strongest Case Against**: **Not in record.** (The Bill's text and Statement of Objects and Reasons provide the government's justification but omit parliamentary debates or stakeholder counter-arguments).

---

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH

* **Gazette Commencement**: Verify whether the notification appointing the commencement date under Clause 1(2) was subsequently issued in the Official Gazette [1].
* **Standing & Registration Criteria**: Track the compliance of consumer associations with registration requirements under the Companies Act, 1956 or applicable Societies/Trust registration laws to establish legal locus standi before Special Courts [4].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006** (enacted as **The Aircraft (Amendment) Act, 2007**, Act No. 44 of 2007) amends the **Aircraft Act, 1934** [1] [2]. It aligns domestic civil aviation regulations with standards under the **Chicago Convention** (Convention on International Civil Aviation) [3] [4]. The instrument expands the regulatory ambit over foreign-registered aircraft flying in or over India, formalises safety oversight by aviation authorities, extends rulemaking over air traffic control and satellite navigation, and sharpens penal deterrence for aviation offences [2] [3] [5].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Administration:** The Central Government through the **Ministry of Civil Aviation** / **Director-General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)** [1] [6].
* **Statutory vs Executive:** Statutory amendment to the principal Aircraft Act, 1934 [1] [2].
* **Legislative Stage & History:**
  * Passed by the Lok Sabha: **10 September 2007** (11th Session, 14th LS) [4].
  * Passed by the Rajya Sabha: **27 November 2007** (212th Session) [4].
  * Received Presidential Assent: **5 December 2007**; published in the Gazette of India on **6 December 2007** [2] [7].
  * Commencement: Section 1 provides that it comes into force on such date as the Central Government appoints by notification in the Official Gazette (status in parliamentary tracker noted as **Awaited** at enactment) [2] [4].

### 3. DESIGN & KEY CLAUSES
| Provision / Section | Focus | Legal Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Section 1(2)** amended by **Section 2** | Extended Territorial & Operator Scope | Extends the Act to: (c) aircraft registered outside India, and persons on board, while in or over India; and (d) aircraft operated by a non-citizen whose principal place of business or permanent residence is in India [2] [6]. |
| **Section 4A** (New Insertion) | Safety Oversight Functions | Authorises the **Director-General of Civil Aviation** (DGCA), or any other officer specially empowered by the Central Government, to perform safety oversight functions specified in the Act or rules [6] [8]. |
| **Section 5(2)** amended | Expanded Central Rule-Making Powers | Introduces powers to make rules for: aerodrome licensing/inspection and fees where the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 does not apply; **licensing of air traffic control personnel** [clause (ga)]; **certification, inspection, and regulation of communication, navigation, surveillance, and air traffic management (CNS/ATM)** [clause (gb)]; and **measures safeguarding civil aviation against unlawful interference** [clause (gc)] [5] [9]. |
| **Section 5A** amended | DGCA Direction Powers | Enlarges the scope and power of the DGCA (or empowered officers) to issue binding operational directions covering CNS/ATM facilities, aerodrome maintenance, air traffic control, and civil aviation security [8] [10]. |
| Objects & Reasons Scope | Accident & Incident Investigations | Integrates investigation of civil aviation incidents alongside accidents [3]. |

### 4. PENALTIES
The amendment explicitly enhances the quantum of statutory penalties to establish an effective deterrent [3] [11]:
* **Carriage of Arms/Explosives & False Information (Section 10 amended):** Increases penalties for violating rules relating to the carriage of arms or explosives on aircraft, abetment of offences, providing false information, or non-compliance with directions [3] [11].
* **Dangerous / Wilful Flying (Section 11 amended):** Enhances the penalty for wilfully flying an aircraft in a manner causing danger to persons or property on land, on water, or in the air [11].
* **Airport Obstruction & Tree/Building Directions (Section 11B amended):** Enhances penal provisions for failing to comply with Central Government directions issued under Section 9A prohibiting or regulating the construction of buildings or planting of trees near aerodromes [11].
* **Chicago Convention Contraventions:** Imposes statutory penal sanctions for contravening Chicago Convention standards [3].
*(Exact revised rupee caps and prison term ceilings for each specific amended clause are **Not in record.**)*

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Subordinate Legislation:** Promulgation of updated statutory rules governing air traffic controller licensing and CNS/ATM satellite navigation certifications under amended Section 5(2) [5].
* **Safety Oversight Enforcement:** Issuance and operationalisation of binding security and safety directions by the DGCA under Section 4A and Section 5A [8] [10].
* **Enforcement on Foreign Operators:** Oversight mechanisms regarding foreign-registered aircraft flying over Indian airspace and non-citizen operators with Indian business bases under amended Section 1(2) [2] [6].

### WHAT IT IS
**The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006** (enacted as **The Aircraft (Amendment) Act, 2007**, Act No. 44 of 2007) amends the **Aircraft Act, 1934** to update India's civil aviation framework in alignment with standards laid down by the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) and the Chicago Convention [1, 2, 3]. It expands regulatory jurisdiction to foreign-registered aircraft operating in or over India, statutorily empowers safety oversight functions, broadens rule-making powers over air traffic control and communication/navigation facilities, mandates measures against unlawful interference, covers the investigation of "incidents" alongside accidents, and significantly increases penal deterrence [1, 4, 5, 6].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Administration**: Administered by the **Central Government** (Ministry of Civil Aviation) through the **Director-General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)** or officers specially empowered by the Central Government [4, 7].
* **Instrument & Bill Number**: Bill No. **61 of 2006** [3].
* **Legislative Stage & Timeline**:
  * **Introduced in Lok Sabha**: **7 August 2006** [3].
  * **Referred to Standing Committee**: Referred to the Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture on **4 September 2006**; report laid on **13 March 2007** [3].
  * **Passed Lok Sabha**: **10 September 2007** [3].
  * **Passed Rajya Sabha**: **27 November 2007** [3].
  * **President's Assent**: **5 December 2007** (published in the Gazette of India on **6 December 2007**) [2, 8].
  * **Commencement**: To come into force on such date as appointed by Central Government notification in the Official Gazette (marked *Awaited* in the legislative summary record) [2, 3].

### DESIGN & KEY CLAUSES
* **Jurisdictional Expansion (Clause/Section 2)**: Amends Section 1(2) of the principal Act by inserting clauses (c) and (d) to extend applicability:
  * To, and to persons on, aircraft registered outside India but for the time being in or over India [2, 4].
  * To aircraft operated by a non-Indian citizen who has their principal place of business or permanent residence in India [4].
* **Safety Oversight (Clause/Section 4)**: Inserts **Section 4A**, formally empowering the **Director-General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)** or any officer specially empowered by the Central Government to perform safety oversight functions [4].
* **Expanded Rule-Making Powers (Clause/Section 5)**: Amends Section 5(2) to insert:
  * Clause (ba): Fees charged at aerodromes where the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 does not apply [9].
  * Clause (ga): Licensing of personnel engaged in air traffic control [1, 9].
  * Clause (gb): Certification, inspection, and regulation of communication, navigation, surveillance, or air traffic management (CNS/ATM) facilities [1, 9].
  * Clause (gc): Safeguards and security measures to protect civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference [1, 9].
* **Delegated Directions (Clause/Section 6)**: Amends Section 5A to enlarge DGCA's powers to issue statutory directions covering air traffic control, aerodrome maintenance/operations, CNS/ATM facilities, and aviation security [9, 10].
* **Investigation of Incidents (Clause/Section 7)**: Amends Section 7 to include the investigation of an **"incident"** alongside accidents [1, 6].

### PENALTIES
The amendment substantially enhanced the quantum of fines and terms of imprisonment under the principal Act to establish effective deterrence [5]:

| Provision | Subject Matter | Amended Penalty |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Section 10(1)** | Violation of rules framed under the Act [5, 11] | Fine enhanced up to **₹10 lakh** (previously a general fine) [11]. |
| **Section 10(1A)** | Carriage of arms/explosives, furnishing false info, abetment, or non-compliance with directions [5, 11] | Imprisonment up to **3 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both (raised from 1 year or ₹2,000 fine) [11]. |
| **Section 10(2)** | General offences / failure to comply with Section 4 or Section 7 [11, 12] | Imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both (raised from 3 months or ₹1,000 fine) [12]. |
| **Section 11** | Wilfully flying an aircraft causing danger to persons/property on land, water, or in air [5, 12] | Imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both (raised from 6 months or ₹1,000 fine) [12]. |
| **Section 11A** | Flying an aircraft in contravention of orders under Section 6 [12] | Imprisonment enhanced from 6 months to **2 years** [12]. |
| **Section 11B** | Failure to comply with building/tree obstacle directions under Section 9A [5, 13] | Imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both (raised from 6 months or ₹1,000 fine) [13]. |

### TRADE-OFFS

### WHAT IT IS
The **Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006** (enacted as the **Aircraft (Amendment) Act, 2007**, Act No. 44 of 2007) amends the **Aircraft Act, 1934** to update India's civil aviation framework in line with standards established by the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) and the Chicago Convention [1, 2, 20]. It extends statutory jurisdiction over foreign-registered aircraft operating in or over Indian airspace, empowers regulatory oversight over modern satellite-based communication, navigation, surveillance, and air traffic management (CNS/ATM) systems, expands investigation powers to cover incidents alongside accidents, and sharply increases deterrence by enhancing penal provisions [7, 11, 14, 20, 45].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Regulatory Body:** Administered primarily by the **Central Government** (Ministry of Civil Aviation) alongside the **Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)** [11, 14, 39].
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory enactment amending the principal Aircraft Act, 1934 [1, 2].
* **Legislative Stage & Dates:**
  * **Bill Number:** Bill No. 61 of 2006 [20].
  * **Introduced:** Lok Sabha on **7 August 2006** [20].
  * **Standing Committee:** Referred to the Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture on **4 September 2006**; report presented/laid on **13 March 2007** [20].
  * **Passed:** Lok Sabha on **10 September 2007**; Rajya Sabha on **27 November 2007** [19, 20].
  * **President's Assent:** Received assent on **5 December 2007** (published in the Gazette of India on **6 December 2007**) [2, 12].
  * **Commencement:** To come into force on such date as appointed by the Central Government via notification in the Official Gazette (indicated in the legislative tracker as date awaited at publication) [2, 19, 20].

| Section / Clause | Core Subject & Statutory Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Section 1(2)** (amended by Section 2) | Expands the scope of the Act to foreign-registered aircraft (and persons aboard) for the time being in or over India, and to aircraft operated by non-citizens with a principal place of business or permanent residence in India [2, 14]. |
| **Section 4A** (inserted by Section 4) | Explicitly empowers the **Director General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)**, or an officer specially empowered by the Central Government, to carry out safety oversight functions [14, 39]. |
| **Section 5(2)** (amended by Section 5) | Expands Central Government rule-making power to cover: licensing/regulation of aerodromes and fees at non-AAI aerodromes (clauses *b, ba*); licensing of air traffic control personnel (clause *ga*); certification, inspection, and regulation of CNS/ATM facilities (clause *gb*); and safeguards against unlawful interference (clause *gc*) [15]. |
| **Section 5A** (amended by Section 6) | Broadens the DGCA's direction-issuing powers to encompass CNS/ATM facilities, aerodrome maintenance, air traffic control, and civil aviation security [9, 39]. |
| **Section 7** (amended by Section 7) | Extends Central Government rule-making and inquiry powers to the investigation of **incidents** in addition to accidents [11, 45]. |

### PENALTIES
The amendment substantially enhanced monetary and custodial ceilings across several sections of the Aircraft Act, 1934 to establish deterrence [7, 11]:
* **General Contraventions / Chicago Convention Violations (Section 10):**
  * Section 10(1): Unspecified fine enhanced to a fine extending up to **₹10 lakh** [42].
  * Section 10(1A) (carriage of arms, explosives, providing false information, abetment): Increased from imprisonment up to 1 year or fine to imprisonment up to **3 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both [7, 42, 50].
  * Section 10(2) (breach of rules under sections 4 or 7): Increased from imprisonment up to 3 months or fine up to ₹1,000 to imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both [50].
* **Endangerment / Dangerous Flying (Section 11):** Wilfully flying an aircraft causing danger to person or property on land, water, or air increased from 6 months or ₹1,000 fine to imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine extending up to **₹10 lakh**, or both [7, 50].
* **Non-compliance with Airport Obstruction Directions (Section 11B):** Failure to comply with building/tree height restriction directions under section 9A increased from 6 months or ₹1,000 fine to imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine extending up to **₹10 lakh**, or both [7, 47].
* **Section 11A:** Imprisonment ceiling raised from 6 months to **2 years** [50].

* **Strongest Case For (Record):** India's aviation sector had expanded significantly after deregulation in 1994, with navigation and air traffic control migrating to satellite-based CNS/ATM systems; formal statutory authority was necessary to fulfill ICAO standards, establish safety oversight, close jurisdictional loopholes over foreign aircraft in Indian airspace, and deter non-compliance via meaningful penalties [7, 20, 22].

According to the Statement of Objects and Reasons, Lakshadweep lacked a democratic structure, with powers concentrated in the Administrator / Lieutenant Governor and the bureaucracy [3]. - **Service Penalties:** The Central Government and competent administrative authorities hold the power to deny **increments**, stall **promotions**, and restrict **Leave Travel Concessions (LTC)** for personnel in Central Government service, public sector undertakings, or controlled establishments who procreate more than two children [7][8].
